newsitem.title: UK: British court backs Co-op in pursuing its foes.
newsitem.headline: British court backs Co-op in pursuing its foes.

text.p: Britain's

Co-operative Wholesale Society (CWS) on Friday got overwhelming support in its legal action against predator Andrew Regan and his backers when a judge extended an injunction against the use of confidential CWS information and awarded it costs.

Regan's ambitious plan to convert the mutually-owned 153-year-old supermarkets to funeral parlours group into a limited company and sell off some of its businesses collapsed on Thursday after the Co-op refused to countenance his proposals and a City backer withdrew its financing for the 1.2 billion pound ($1.9 billion) bid.

Mr. Justice Lightman said the case in which Regan was fed CWS documents by CWS director Allan Green on which to mount his bid for the Co-op represented a "gross, wilful and disgraceful breach of confidence".
Lightman extended the injunction on the use of the information until the full hearing of CWS claim for damages.

He also awarded punitive "indemnity" costs -- described by one legal source as the highest level available -- against Regan, his business associate David Lyons, suspended CWS director Green and Regan's companies Lanica Trust and specially-formed bidding vehicle Galileo.

Christopher Clarke QC, the lawyer representing the CWS, told the court how affidavits provided by Green, Regan and Lyons under the terms of an order issued last week showed Green had passed on papers including CWS profit forecasts, the board budget and the board's defence plan to 1997 to Regan and Lyons.

Clarke said 32 documents had been handed over to the court, including the entire CWS membership list. He said Green's affidavit revealed he had met with Regan and Lyons on six or seven occasions and had handed over papers at most of these meetings.
The court was told Green had agreed he had exceeded his authority but believed at the time he was doing so in the best interest of CWS.

Clarke also said copies of some of the documents had been passed on to Galileo's City advisor British merchant bank Hambros and a long list of other organisations, including banks and financial institutions.

Retailer Sainsbury, Nomura, property consultant Healey and Baker, Leucadia National Corp., UBS, SocGen, Goldman Sachs, J.P. Morgan, HSBC Investment Bank, Lloyds Bank, Lloyds Bank Registrars, Bankers Trust, Avon Wick Ltd, accountancy firm Price Waterhouse and Hillier Parker were all named.
Shareholders of Lanica had also shown documents to British investment watchdog IMRO.
The injunction was extended to cover Hambros and City law firm Travers Smith Braithwaite.
CWS spokesman Bill Shannon told Reuters that the judge's ruling and the evidence gained as a result of the court order justified its actions.

"We totally agree with what the judge said. I don't think he could have expressed it better. We made it clear in February that no part of the CWS was for sale. What we have seen is that our values and principles are not shared by some people in the City," he said.

Earlier in the proceedings, when the lawyer representing Regan, Lyons, Galileo and Lanica said it was unfortunate the bid had never been presented to the CWS members, Judge Lightman said "it was inevitable that it should be stopped due to the iniquitous manner in which it was done".

CWS has waged a high-profile defence since the bid attempt first surfaced in February. This intensified last week when it suspended two senior managers, Green and David Chambers, for a serious breach of trust and later won a court order preventing the predators from using any of the information they had obtained through Green.

This effectively stopped the bid in its tracks, although it was not until Thursday that Regan and Galileo admitted defeat, blaming the fact that CWS chairman had not allowed them to put their proposals directly to CWS directors. These proposals were returned unopened and unread to Galileo.
CWS has also said it will begin a private prosecution against 31-year-old entrepreneur Regan and Lyons as well as action accusing Green of theft.
"We are not finished," CWS spokesman Shannon told Reuters when asked if the court ruling marked the end of the affair. ($ = 0.616 British Pounds)
